say: You give it a growth or decay with two readings, like the amount at $t=0$ and the amount at a later time. It finds the constants in the model, $A$ and $k$ (or $a$ and $b$), so you can **predict** any other time.
The key idea: the starting reading gives $A$ straight away. The second reading leaves an exponential on its own, and taking logs brings the power down so you can solve for the constant.

how.ordinary: On Ordinary Level it came up once, in Paper 1 in 2023, as a 5-mark part: put a known value into the model $y = a \times b^x$ and solve for $a$.

example.question: The number of bacteria in a dish is modelled by $P(t) = A e^{kt}$, where $t$ is the time in hours. At $t = 0$ there are $80$ bacteria. At $t = 4$ there are $500$. Find $A$ and $k$, and use the model to predict the number of bacteria at $t = 10$.

steps.title: Find A from t = 0
steps.say: At $t = 0$ the power is $e^0 = 1$, so $\hl{1}{A}$ is just the starting number.

steps.title: Use the second reading
steps.say: Put $t = 4$ and $P = 500$ into the model, then divide by $\hl{1}{80}$ to leave the exponential on its own.

steps.title: Take logs to find k
steps.say: Take $\ln$ of both sides. $\ln$ undoes $e$, so the $4k$ comes down. Then divide by $4$ to get $\hl{2}{k}$.

steps.title: Predict at t = 10
steps.say: Keep $\hl{2}{k}$ exact so no rounding error creeps in. Put $t = 10$ into $P(t) = \hl{1}{80}\,e^{\hl{2}{k}t}$.

ordinary.tip: Do not round a power like $0.83^{14}$ early. Keep the full calculator value until the last step.
Substituting the known values into the model earns partial credit even if you stop there. Write the substitution out.
Round the final answer. An answer that is not rounded, or is rounded wrongly, loses a mark.

say: You give it a diagram with two straight lines crossing and an angle you do not know. It finds the unknown and gives the **reason** the marks are tied to.
The key idea: when two lines cross, the angles facing each other across the crossing point are **vertically opposite**, and they are always equal.

how.higher: Higher Level uses it on Paper 2 in five of the eleven years, always as a reason inside a longer proof, for example one of the angles that makes two triangles congruent.
how.ordinary: Ordinary Level used it as a step in Paper 2 in 2020 and 2025, for finding unknown angles, never as the main skill.

example.question: Two straight lines cross at a point. One angle is $(3x + 10)°$. The angle vertically opposite it is $(5x - 30)°$. Find $x$ and the size of the angle $(3x + 10)°$.

steps.title: Spot the equal pair
steps.say: These two angles face each other across the crossing point, so they are **vertically opposite**. Vertically opposite angles are equal.

lines.text: Reason: vertically opposite angles are equal.

steps.title: Solve for x
steps.say: Collect the $\hl{1}{x}$ terms on one side and the numbers on the other.

lines.text: Check with the other angle: $5(20) - 30 = 70$. They match.

say: You give it a triangle with some angles known and one unknown. It finds the missing angle and names the **reason**.
The key idea: the three angles of any triangle add to $180°$, so the unknown is $180°$ minus the others.

how.higher: Higher Level uses it in seven Paper 2 parts, as a short step inside bigger questions: finding the angle you need before the sine rule, or inside a circle-geometry proof.
how.ordinary: Ordinary Level uses it most: thirteen Paper 2 parts, four of them with it as the main skill, such as the 10-mark part finding three angles in 2025 or the 5-mark part finding an angle in 2025 Q2.

example.question: The angles of a triangle are $(2x + 10)°$, $(3x - 20)°$ and $70°$. Find $x$ and the size of the other two angles.

steps.title: State the rule
steps.say: The three angles of a triangle add to $180°$. Write them all added together.

lines.text: Reason: angles in a triangle add to $180°$.

steps.title: Simplify
steps.say: Add the $\hl{1}{x}$ terms, then add the numbers.

say: You give it two parallel lines cut by a third line, and one angle you do not know. It finds the angle and gives the **reason**.

The key idea: **alternate angles** sit on opposite sides of the cutting line, between the parallels, and are equal. They form a Z shape. The reverse also works: equal alternate angles prove the lines parallel.

how.higher: Higher Level uses it in six Paper 2 parts, as one of the reasons in a congruent-triangle or similar-triangle proof.
how.ordinary: Ordinary Level used it in Paper 2 in 2015 (Q4(a), finding $x$, $y$ and $z$ with a reason for each) and in 2020 Q5(c).

example.question: The lines $l$ and $m$ are parallel and are cut by a third line. The angle $(4x - 15)°$ on $l$ and the angle $(2x + 25)°$ on $m$ are alternate. Find $x$ and the size of the angle $(4x - 15)°$.

steps.title: Spot the equal pair
steps.say: The angles are on opposite sides of the cutting line and between the parallels, a Z shape. **Alternate angles** are equal.

lines.text: Reason: alternate angles are equal ($l \parallel m$).

steps.title: Solve for x
steps.say: Collect the $\hl{1}{x}$ terms on one side and the numbers on the other.

higher.tip: Write "alternate angles" as the reason next to the equal angles. Statements need their reasons for full marks.
You only need two correct reasons out of the steps S1 to S3, so a clear reason on each angle you use is enough.
Listing the steps without any justification stops you short of full marks. Name the justification for each.

ordinary.tip: A value with its reason earns more than a value on its own. Write the reason beside each answer.
Full marks need correct values and a reason for each.
